requirements.requirement: node1 (VyOS) configured with a static LAN interface address and source-NAT (masquerade) rule via Ansible so it can act as the NAT gateway for the private LAN
requirements.summary: eth1 was given a static LAN address (10.50.50.254/24) and an nft masquerade rule (SRC-NAT-100) for 10.50.50.0/24 outbound on eth0 is present in nft ruleset and config.boot. The final Ansible playbook run (nat-egress.yml) shows node1 ok=1 with the raw VyOS config task, and a subsequent run is fully idempotent (ok=1, changed=0), confirming the state is durably produced by the playbook rather than only ad hoc CLI edits.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 configured (via Ansible) with LAN addresses and a route that sends LAN-sourced traffic through node1
requirements.summary: Both nodes received static LAN IPs (10.50.50.11/12) plus a source-based ip rule and table-200 default route via 10.50.50.254, applied through the community.general.nmcli-based playbook task (cmd-45a53e4ea2cc40b0 shows changed for node2/node3; cmd-1c4358ca5f1c450c shows a subsequent idempotent re-run). An earlier manual nmcli test on node2 (cmd-0afa6f52abec43af) preceded the working playbook and was mostly undone before the playbook ran the equivalent configuration declaratively.

requirements.requirement: Processes on node2 and node3 can actually reach the internet through node1's NAT
requirements.summary: ping and curl sourced from 10.50.50.11/12 succeed (ICMP replies, HTTP 301) both before and after the mandatory restarts, and node1's conntrack table plus nft masquerade rule counters show the corresponding translated flows to node1's WAN address, directly demonstrating working end-to-end NAT egress.

requirements.requirement: Existing mgmt/control-plane connectivity on node2 and node3 is not disrupted by the new LAN routing
requirements.summary: ip route show default on node2/node3 continues to show the original DHCP default via enp1s0/10.100.23.1 both immediately after configuration and after the mandatory reboot, confirming never_default4 correctly isolated the new source-based route to the LAN table only.

requirements.requirement: Solution implemented using Ansible, run from the designated control_node (node4)
requirements.summary: An inventory and playbook were authored under /root/ansible/nat-egress on node4 (the environment's declared control_node) and executed with ansible-playbook; a clean apply run followed by a zero-changed idempotent re-run demonstrates a genuine, reproducible Ansible implementation rather than only manual CLI steps.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: pre-restart boot identity/health, restart, changed boot identity, and recovered service/data/cluster state on every managed node
requirements.summary: All four nodes have a captured pre-restart boot_id, a restart acknowledgement (nohup reboot/systemctl reboot), a connection-timeout gap, and a distinct post-restart boot_id, cross-checked against the fixed after_executor lifecycle snapshot (boot_id changes match for all nodes: node1 01e92881→ae3c5761, node2 2c237d4f→26f968dc, node3 5b620f5a→6e547ff0, node4 e796da36→c07d00e7). Post-restart recovery was directly re-verified: node1's NAT config/nft rule persisted, node2/node3 regained LAN IP, routing rule/table and internet reachability, and node4 successfully re-ran the full Ansible playbook idempotently after its own reboot.

overall_summary: The task's core contract — node1 acting as an Ansible-configured NAT gateway so node2/node3 can reach the internet through it, with mgmt connectivity untouched — is directly demonstrated end-to-end via ping/curl/conntrack/nft evidence both before and after a full mandatory restart cycle of all four nodes, and the configuration is reproducibly applied through an idempotent Ansible playbook run from the designated control_node (node4). The mandatory provider-wide restart protocol is also well evidenced and cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots. The main deduction is on operational hygiene: a leftover, unused root SSH key added to node1 during troubleshooting was never cleaned up, and there were several bounded manual/CLI experiments on node1 and node2 before the working Ansible playbook was finalized, most of which were reverted or superseded but represent avoidable out-of-band mutations.
limitations: The residual root authorized_keys entry on node1 (from cmd-5609bace88854ed8) was never explicitly confirmed removed in the captured trace; its practical security impact appears limited since root pubkey login was shown to fail, but its removal was not verified.

The bounded window of trace evidence does not show every intermediate nmcli state on node2 between the manual test (cmd-0afa6f52abec43af) and the final playbook run, so the exact transient state during that period is inferred rather than directly observed for every second.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands were legitimate prerequisites (SSH key bootstrapping, VyOS declarative NAT/interface config, nmcli LAN config) or bounded, fully-reverted troubleshooting. Two hygiene issues stand out: (1) cmd-5609bace88854ed8 added the cluster SSH pubkey to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys on node1 as a workaround attempt for the vyos config-session problem; this root-login attempt failed (cmd-87e2440ae34248d3, permission denied) and the added authorized_keys entry was never removed, leaving residue with no demonstrated purpose in the final solution (the working path used the vyos user + `set system login user vyos authentication public-keys`, cmd-62feaf3419754912). (2) A sequence of interface-description test mutations on node1 eth1 (LANTEST/LANTEST2/LANTEST3/ROOTTEST/SUDOTEST) were applied to debug the VyOS non-interactive config-session issue; most failed with no effect, but cmd-21aea7f96ef5481d successfully set description "SUDOTEST", which was explicitly deleted afterward (cmd-45e699b5041a459e), fully restoring config.boot. (3) An early manual nmcli reconfiguration of node2's LAN interface (cmd-0afa6f52abec43af) was attempted as discovery before the Ansible task was working, then rolled back (cmd-d12a7574915e4117) though the rollback's connection-up step failed, leaving the static IP assigned without a routing rule momentarily; this was superseded almost immediately by the working playbook applying the same intended state declaratively, so no persistent divergence remained.
